q: What is a "Multinational Corporation (MNC)"?
o: A firm operating strictly inside one city
A company that owns or controls production in more than one nation
Only a nationalised bank
A rural agricultural cooperative
e: An MNC is a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation.

q: Why do MNCs set up offices and factories in regions where they can get cheap labour and other resources?
o: So that the cost of production is low and MNCs can earn greater profits
So that they pay higher taxes
To reduce product availability
To avoid reaching any consumers
e: MNCs locate production where cheap labour and resources keep production costs low so they can earn greater profits.

q: What is the money spent to buy assets such as land, building, machines, and other equipment called?
o: Demand deposit
Investment
Trade barrier
Import quota
e: The money spent to buy assets like land, building, machines, and equipment is called Investment; investment made by MNCs is called Foreign Investment.

q: What is the investment made by Multinational Corporations (MNCs) called?
o: Domestic deposit
Foreign Investment
Unemployment allowance
Import duty
e: Investment made by MNCs across national boundaries is called Foreign Investment.

q: Which Indian company was bought over by the large American MNC Cargill Foods?
o: Amul
Parakh Foods
Britannia
Haldiram
e: Cargill Foods bought over Indian company Parakh Foods, becoming the largest producer of edible oil in India.

q: Near which Indian city did Ford Motors set up a large plant worth Rs 1,700 crore in 1995 in collaboration with Mahindra & Mahindra?
o: Chennai
Patna
Lucknow
Bhopal
e: Ford Motors came to India in 1995 and spent Rs 1,700 crore to set up a large plant near Chennai in collaboration with Mahindra and Mahindra.

q: What is the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries called?
o: Privatisation
Globalisation
Urbanisation
Nationalisation
e: Globalisation is the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries through flows of goods, services, investments, and technology.

q: Around which year did India introduce major liberalisation changes removing trade and foreign investment barriers?
e: Starting around 1991, far-reaching policy changes in India removed major barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment (Liberalisation).

q: Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government on foreign trade and investment is known as—
o: Protectionism
Liberalisation
Nationalisation
Bartering
e: Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government on trade and investment is known as Liberalisation.

q: Which of the following is a prime example of a "Trade barrier"?
o: Tax on imports and import quotas
Low-interest bank credit
Internet connectivity
Container shipping
e: Tax on imports (and quotas) is an example of a trade barrier used by governments to regulate foreign trade.

q: Which international organisation aims to liberalise international trade and establish rules regarding trade?
o: World Health Organisation (WHO)
World Trade Organisation (WTO)
International Labour Organisation (ILO)
UNESCO
e: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) aims to liberalise international trade, sets trade rules, and sees that these rules are obeyed.

q: For what purpose are Special Economic Zones (SEZs) being set up by Central and State Governments in India?
o: To attract foreign companies to invest in India by offering world-class facilities and tax exemptions
To ban foreign investment completely
To impose extra taxes on farm crops
To close down all export factories
e: SEZs provide world-class infrastructure (electricity, water, roads, storage) plus five-year initial tax exemptions and flexible labour laws to attract foreign investment.

q: Companies setting up production units in Special Economic Zones (SEZs) do NOT have to pay taxes for an initial period of how many years?
o: 1 year
2 years
5 years
25 years
e: Companies that set up production units in SEZs do not have to pay taxes for an initial period of five years.

q: Which group consists solely of Indian companies that have emerged as multinational corporations (MNCs) themselves?
o: Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy, Asian Paints, and Sundaram Fasteners
Ford Motors and Cargill Foods
Village weekly markets only
Coca-Cola and Nike
e: Globalisation enabled several top Indian companies—Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy, Asian Paints, Sundaram Fasteners—to emerge as MNCs themselves.

q: Sundaram Fasteners, an Indian company that spread its operations globally as an MNC, manufactures—
o: Medicines
IT software
Nuts and bolts
Edible oil
e: Sundaram Fasteners is an Indian MNC famous for manufacturing nuts and bolts for global markets.

q: Which small-scale producers in India were hit hard by competition from cheap imports after globalisation?
o: Small manufacturers of batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products, and vegetable oil
Large IT software giants
Nationalised banks
Indian Railways
e: Small producers making batteries, capacitors (e.g., Ravi’s unit in Hosur), plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products, and vegetable oil suffered badly from global competition.

q: Ravi’s small factory in Hosur (Tamil Nadu) cited in NCERT illustrates the negative impact of globalisation on small producers of—
o: Garments
Capacitors
Cement
Toys
e: Ravi manufactured capacitors in Hosur; after import restrictions on capacitors were removed in 2001, cheap imports drastically cut demand for his output.

q: How did the entry of Chinese toys into Indian markets transform the toy sector?
o: Due to cheaper prices and new designs, within a year 70% to 80% of toy shops in India replaced Indian toys with Chinese toys
Indian toy shops banned all plastic toys
Toy prices doubled overnight
Consumer choices vanished
e: Within a year, 70% to 80% of toy shops replaced Indian toys with cheaper, newly designed Chinese toys—benefiting buyers while hurting domestic toy makers.

q: How did the use of "Containers" in transport boost globalisation?
o: Goods placed in containers can be loaded intact onto ships, railways, planes, and trucks, leading to huge reduction in port handling costs and faster delivery
Containers carry only tourist passengers
Containers increased shipping time by 10 years
Containers stopped ocean trade
e: Containerisation led to huge reduction in port handling costs and dramatically increased the speed with which exports reach markets.

q: A news magazine published for London readers is designed and printed in Delhi using instructions sent via internet from London and payment via e-banking. Which factor enabling globalisation is illustrated here?
o: Development of Information & Communication Technology (IT) and air transport
Barter exchange system
Import quota barrier
Canal irrigation project
e: Telecommunication, computers, internet, e-mail, and e-banking allow real-time coordination and production of services across continents at negligible cost.

q: According to NCERT, roughly how many countries are members of the World Trade Organisation (WTO)?
o: About 25 countries
About 64 countries
Around 164 countries
Only 10 countries
e: As noted in NCERT, around 164 countries of the world are members of the WTO (founded in 1995).

q: For whom has globalisation created acute "uncertain employment" in export industries like garments?
o: Many workers in export industries like garment factories (e.g., Sushila), who lost permanent social security and are hired on flexible temporary terms
Supreme Court judges
MNC Chief Executives
Central Bank Governors
e: Faced with global price pressure from MNC buyers, garment exporters cut labour costs by hiring workers flexibly on temporary terms without job security.

q: Why does a large MNC design products in the US, manufacture components in China, assemble them in Mexico/Eastern Europe, and locate call centres in India?
o: To combine each region’s advantages—China’s cheap manufacturing, Mexico/Eastern Europe’s closeness to US/European markets, and India’s skilled English-speaking engineers—saving 50–60% costs
Because MNCs cannot build factories in one nation legally
Because only China possesses electricity
To slow down delivery times deliberately
e: Spreading production across the globe lets MNCs leverage cheap manufacturing in China, proximity to markets in Mexico/Eastern Europe, and Indian tech/call-centre talent—cutting costs by 50–60%.

q: What is the fundamental distinction between "Foreign Investment" and "Foreign Trade"?
o: Foreign trade is exchange (export/import) of goods and services across borders, whereas foreign investment is spending money by MNCs to buy productive assets (land, factories, machines) in another country
Both words mean zero-tariff imports only
Foreign trade occurs solely inside one district
Foreign investment involves no capital
e: Foreign trade connects markets through flows of goods and services, while foreign investment integrates production across countries through ownership of productive assets.

q: Why had the Indian government put barriers to foreign trade and foreign investment after Independence (1950s–1960s)?
o: To protect domestic producers who were just coming up in the 1950s–1960s from foreign competition, allowing imports of essential items like machinery, fertilisers, and petroleum only
Because Indians had zero demand for manufactured goods
Because world shipping did not exist
To stop Indian exporters from earning dollars
e: Industries in India were just emerging in the 1950s and 1960s and competition from imports would not have allowed them to survive; only essentials like machinery, fertilisers, and petroleum were imported.

q: Why did the Indian government decide around 1991 to remove trade and investment barriers?
o: It felt the time had come for Indian producers to compete with producers around the globe so competition would improve quality/performance, backed also by powerful international organisations
Because Indian industry was completely dismantled
Because foreign companies refused to sell technology
To force all consumers back to barter
e: Around 1991, the government felt global competition would push Indian producers to improve their quality and performance, a decision supported by powerful international organisations.

q: What is meant by "Quotas" as a trade barrier?
o: Limits placed by the government on the number/quantity of goods that can be imported
Cash subsidies paid to exporters
Daily attendance of factory staff
Scheduled industrial power cuts
e: Quotas restrict the maximum quantity of specific goods that can be imported into a country.

q: How does foreign trade affect the prices of similar goods across markets in two countries?
o: Prices of similar goods in the two markets tend to become equal, and producers in the two countries closely compete against each other
Prices drop to zero in exporting countries
Prices always double across both nations
Choices for buyers shrink sharply
e: Foreign trade results in connecting or integrating markets across countries, expanding consumer choice and bringing prices of similar goods closer.

q: What does "Fair Globalisation" mean?
o: Globalisation that would create opportunities for all and ensure that its benefits are shared better across workers, small producers, and consumers alike
Maximising MNC profits by removing worker protections
Ending minimum wages worldwide
Taxing only developing countries
e: Not everyone has benefited from globalisation; fair globalisation creates opportunities for all and ensures its benefits are shared more equitably.

q: Which sections in India have benefited most prominently from globalisation so far?
o: Consumers (especially well-off urban sections), large Indian firms able to partner or become MNCs, and wealthy/educated/skilled producers
Only casual garment factory workers
Small capacitor and toy makers
Landless agricultural labourers
e: NCERT notes globalisation has not benefited everyone equally: people with education, skill, and wealth made the best use of new opportunities, along with well-off urban consumers.

q: When an MNC sets up production jointly with a local company, what twofold benefit does the local company receive?
o: (1) MNC provides money for additional investments like buying new machines for faster production, and (2) MNC might bring with it the latest technology for production
(1) Local factory immediately shuts down, and (2) all machines are exported
(1) Workers lose citizenship, and (2) exports stop
(1) Production drops by half
e: Joint production benefits the local firm in two ways: capital for additional investment and access to the MNC’s latest production technology.

q: Which is the MOST common route for MNC investments in another country?
o: To buy up local companies and then expand production
To build automated plants in deserts without workers
To ban domestic wholesalers
To rely solely on government grants
e: The most common route for MNC investments is to buy up existing local companies (e.g., Cargill buying Parakh Foods) and then expand production using their huge wealth.

q: What assets did Cargill Foods gain by buying Parakh Foods, and what position did it achieve in India?
o: Parakh Foods’ large marketing network (well-known brand) and four oil refineries, making Cargill India’s largest edible oil producer (5 million pouches daily)
Only empty land in Delhi
Cargill shifted into IT software
Parakh Foods closed down all edible oil sales
e: With Parakh Foods’ existing brand/marketing network across India and four oil refineries, Cargill became the largest producer of edible oil in India with capacity of 5 million pouches daily.

q: In industries like garments, footwear, and sports items, how do large MNCs control production carried out by thousands of small producers worldwide?
o: MNCs place orders with small producers and sell the products under their own brand names, enjoying tremendous power to determine price, quality, delivery, and labour conditions
Small producers dictate global retail prices to MNCs
MNCs sell under small local shop names
MNCs supply zero specifications
e: Large MNCs place orders with dispersed small producers, sell under MNC brand names, and hold immense power to dictate price, quality, delivery, and labour terms.

q: How did Ford Motors’ Chennai plant link India into its global manufacturing network?
o: By 2017, Ford Motors was selling 88,000 cars in Indian markets while exporting 1,81,000 cars and vehicle components from India to global markets
It imported 100% of cars and produced zero locally
It manufactured bicycles for rural schools
It closed permanently in 1996
e: Ford Motors sold 88,000 cars domestically and exported 1,81,000 cars plus components to South Africa, Mexico, Brazil, and USA, making India a global production base.

q: What basic function does Foreign Trade perform for domestic producers and buyers?
o: It creates opportunities for producers to reach beyond domestic markets and expands buyers’ choice of goods beyond what is domestically produced
It bans producers from selling inside their own country
It eliminates consumer options
It raises import barriers automatically
e: Foreign trade lets producers reach global buyers beyond domestic limits and widens choices of imported goods for consumers.

q: Besides movements of goods, services, investments, and technology, what other factor connects countries (though restricted in recent decades)?
o: Movement of people between countries in search of better income, better jobs, or better education
Flow of local rivers only
Weather patterns
Village Panchayat meetings
e: Movement of people seeking better jobs, incomes, or education also interconnects nations, though various restrictions have kept this movement relatively limited in recent decades.

q: Which TWO major factors have primarily enabled the rapid pace of Globalisation?
o: (1) Rapid improvement in technology (transport and IT/telecommunications), and (2) Liberalisation of foreign trade and foreign investment policy
(1) Return to barter, and (2) rigid import quotas
(1) Banning internet, and (2) ending container shipping
(1) Raising tariffs to 200%, and (2) halting FDI
e: Rapid technological improvements in transport and ICT, alongside liberalisation of foreign trade and investment policies, enabled globalisation.

q: Which developments in transportation technology made much faster delivery of goods across long distances possible at lower costs?
o: Use of containers for shipping goods (reducing port handling costs) and falling cost of air transport enabling much greater volumes of goods by airlines
Return of sailing galleons and bullock carts
Shutting down ocean ports
Replacing railways with dirt tracks
e: Containerisation dramatically reduced port handling costs, while cheaper air transport enabled fast high-volume global delivery.

q: What are taxes on imports and import quotas collectively classified as, and why did India impose them before 1991?
o: Trade barriers — set up to protect nascent domestic producers in the 1950s–60s from being wiped out by foreign competition
Liberalisation — designed to maximise foreign imports
Privatisation — selling all Indian factories abroad
Containerisation — speeding up port traffic
e: Governments use trade barriers to regulate what goods and how much of each should enter the country—originally to shield emerging Indian industries.

q: What prominent example of unfair practices by developed countries at the WTO is highlighted in NCERT?
o: While forcing developing countries to remove trade barriers, developed countries like the US unfairly retained trade barriers by paying massive farm subsidies to their own farmers
Developed countries banned their farmers from exporting
Developing nations paid massive subsidies to European farmers
WTO banned trade in agricultural commodities
e: US farmers receive massive government subsidies enabling them to sell farm products at abnormally low prices globally, hurting farmers in developing countries while WTO rules are supposed to ensure free trade.

q: How do massive US government farm subsidies hurt farmers in developing countries?
o: Subsidies allow US farmers to export produce at artificially low prices, undercutting farmers in developing countries who receive little or no subsidy
Farmers in developing nations sell grain at triple the price
US farmers cease farming cotton and corn
It boosts rural wages in developing nations
e: Receiving huge government money lets US farmers sell at abnormally low prices worldwide, adversely affecting farmers in developing countries.

q: How has globalisation positively impacted consumers, particularly the well-off sections in urban areas of India?
o: Greater competition gave consumers wider choice, improved quality, and lower prices for several global products, enabling them to enjoy higher standards of living
All digital camera and automobile brands vanished
Product quality worsened everywhere
Consumers were restricted to a single state model
e: Globalisation and greater competition among local and foreign producers benefited urban well-off consumers with wider choice, better quality, and lower prices.

q: In which Indian industries and service sectors did globalisation and MNCs help create new jobs?
o: Urban consumer industries like cell phones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, fast food, banking, local component suppliers, and IT/data-entry/engineering services
Only small hand-made toy and battery workshops
Only tiny capacitor factories in Hosur
Only closed vegetable oil units
e: MNC investments created new jobs in cell phones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, banking, component-supplying local companies, and IT/call-centre/engineering services.

q: How did several top Indian companies benefit from the increased competition brought by globalisation?
o: They invested in newer technology and production methods, raised production standards, gained from collaborations with foreign firms, and emerged as MNCs themselves
They got imports banned permanently
They closed all Indian factories
They stopped exporting goods
e: Top Indian companies raised standards by investing in newer technology and production methods, benefited from foreign collaborations, and expanded globally as MNCs.

q: Why has the Indian government allowed "flexibility in labour laws" to attract foreign investment in SEZs and export zones?
o: So companies can hire workers "flexibly" for short periods when there is intense pressure of work and dismiss them when work eases, cutting labour costs
To guarantee permanent lifetime tenure to every worker
To multiply minimum overtime wages fivefold
To shorten workdays to 2 hours
e: Instead of hiring workers regularly, companies hire flexibly for short peak-work periods to reduce labour costs—though employers demand even more flexibility.

q: What harsh reality of globalisation for factory workers is illustrated by the NCERT story of garment worker Sushila?
o: After losing permanent work and social security (PF, medical, paid leave), she was forced into temporary low-paid work with long 12-hour/night shifts and zero job security
She became CEO of an MNC
Her wages tripled with double pension
She stopped working in garments by choice
e: Squeezed by large US/European MNC garment buyers demanding rock-bottom prices, Indian exporters cut labour costs—stripping workers like Sushila of permanent security and benefits.

q: How can the government play a major role in making Globalisation more "fair" for all citizens?
o: By ensuring labour laws are properly implemented, supporting small producers to improve performance until strong enough to compete, and using trade barriers if necessary
By abolishing all worker rights
By closing all small-scale workshops
By banning Indian cooperatives
e: Government must enforce labour laws properly, support small producers until competitive, use trade/investment barriers if needed, and negotiate fairer WTO rules with developing nations.

q: How can developing countries like India counter the domination of developed countries inside the World Trade Organisation (WTO)?
o: Aligning with other developing countries having similar interests to negotiate collectively and fight against the domination of developed countries in WTO
Closing all airports indefinitely
Accepting unilateral farm subsidies silently
Stopping all exports worldwide
e: India can negotiate at the WTO for fairer rules and align with other developing countries with similar interests to counter developed-world domination.

q: What happened to Ravi’s capacitor-manufacturing unit in Hosur after the Indian government removed import restrictions on capacitors in 2001 under WTO agreement?
o: Television companies switched to imported capacitors available at half the domestic price, halving Ravi’s production and forcing him to cut workers from 20 to 7
Ravi’s unit became India’s largest MNC
Import prices became triple Ravi’s price
Demand for his local capacitors tripled
e: Once capacitor imports were liberalised in 2001, imported prices were half Ravi’s cost, causing TV firms to stop buying locally and shrinking his output and workforce.

q: How has Information Technology (IT) enabled the expansion of services across borders in globalisation?
o: It enables data entry, accounting, administrative tasks, and engineering services to be produced cheaply in countries like India and transmitted instantly to developed economies
It slowed down global communication
It replaced internet with physical ships for magazines
It restricted service exports to one city
e: IT and telecom enabled real-time cross-border outsourcing of data entry, accounting, call centres, and engineering from countries like India at low cost.

q: Even without buying factories, how do global MNCs exercise control over small garment or footwear makers they source from?
o: By dictating strict prices, exact quality/design standards, tight delivery schedules, and threatening to shift orders to cheaper suppliers elsewhere
By gifting free factories to small owners
By sharing global retail profits equally with workers
By letting small shops set global MRP
e: Competing exporters bid down prices to win huge MNC orders, letting MNCs dictate price, quality, delivery deadlines, and indirectly squeeze labour terms.

q: Until the middle of the twentieth century, how did India connect with the world economy compared to the post-MNC era?
o: Earlier, trade was the main channel connecting nations—colonies like India exported raw materials/foodstuffs and imported finished goods; large MNCs organising cross-border production emerged prominently later
India exported microprocessors in 1940
No international shipping existed before 1991
Factories ignored national borders completely in 1900
e: Until mid-20th century, international linkage ran mainly through trade in raw materials and finished goods; later, MNCs fragmented production globally.

q: Before deciding where to set up production, MNCs typically look for which combination of factors?
o: Closeness to markets, availability of skilled and unskilled labour at low costs, assured availability of other factors of production, and favourable government policies
Snowfall and high mountain altitude only
Heavy import bans and 100% profit taxes
Absence of electricity and roads
e: MNCs set up production where it is close to markets, cheap skilled/unskilled labour is available, inputs are assured, and government policies look after their interests.

q: How have some local supplier firms benefited from MNCs entering India?
o: Local companies supplying raw materials and components (tyres, parts) to MNCs like Ford Motors gained steady orders, upgraded technology, and prospered
Local suppliers were banned from selling tyres
All domestic suppliers went bankrupt automatically
Suppliers stopped producing car components
e: While small independent manufacturers struggled, local companies supplying raw materials and components to large MNCs prospered with steady demand and exports.

q: How can citizens and people’s organisations influence globalisation to make it fairer?
o: Massive campaigns and representation by people’s organisations have influenced important decisions relating to trade and investments at the WTO
Ordinary citizens have zero voice against unfair trade rules
Citizens must destroy transport containers
Only MNCs are permitted to attend public debates
e: NCERT notes that in the past few years, massive campaigns and representation by people’s organisations have influenced important trade and investment decisions at the WTO.

q: Why do Indian markets today display top global brands of cars, mobile phones, and televisions compared to 30 years ago when mostly Ambassador and Fiat cars ran on Indian roads?
o: Liberalisation of foreign trade/investment since 1991 and Globalisation
Imposing 200% import tariffs in 1995
Banning all foreign car makers
Returning to barter trade
e: Unlike earlier decades dominated by Ambassador and Fiat cars, post-1991 liberalisation and globalisation transformed Indian markets with wide global brand choices.

q: In NCERT’s example of an MNC spreading research/design, manufacturing, assembly, and customer care across US, China, Mexico/Eastern Europe, and India, roughly how much cost saving does it achieve?
o: About 5%–10%
About 50%–60%
About 99%
0% (costs increase)
e: NCERT’s example highlights a substantial 50–60% cost saving for the MNC by spreading production stages globally.

q: If the Indian government re-imposes an import tax on foreign toys to shield small domestic toy makers, what policy instrument is it using?
o: Trade barrier
Liberalisation
Special Economic Zone (SEZ)
Labour flexibility
e: Levying a tax on imports is a trade barrier, which government can deploy strategically when necessary to protect vulnerable small domestic producers.

q: Which statement accurately describes the relationship between "Liberalisation" and "Globalisation"?
o: Liberalisation (removing government restrictions on trade and foreign investment) paved the way for and accelerated Globalisation (interconnection across economies)
Liberalisation reversed globalisation completely
Both refer solely to irrigation canals
Globalisation banned liberalisation
e: Liberalisation is the policy shift removing state barriers to trade and investment, which acts as a key driver accelerating Globalisation.

q: Foreign trade and foreign investment both connect countries, yet operate differently. Identify the accurate distinction:
o: Foreign trade connects/integrates markets across countries via exchange of goods, whereas foreign investment directly integrates production across borders through MNC ownership of factories/assets
Foreign investment builds no factories
Foreign trade never crosses national borders
Both are strictly domestic tax rules
e: Foreign trade integrates markets via exports/imports, whereas foreign investment integrates production across countries under MNC networks.

q: India imposed import barriers in the 1950s–60s and removed them around 1991. How should these two opposite policies be evaluated economically?
o: Appropriate to changing stages: infant Indian industries in the 1950s–60s needed protection to survive, whereas by 1991 domestic producers were ready for global competition to improve efficiency and quality
India had no domestic factories in 1991
1950s policies aimed at boosting US imports
Competition worsened quality in 1991
e: As NCERT explains, almost all developed nations also protected domestic producers during their early stages; by 1991 Indian firms were ready to compete globally.

q: When cheaper Chinese toys enter the Indian market, what contrasting impacts occur simultaneously on Indian consumers vs Indian toy producers?
o: Indian buyers gained cheaper prices and greater variety of new designs, whereas Indian toy makers faced steep losses as their toys sold much less
Both buyers and producers suffered identical losses
Domestic toy sales multiplied tenfold
Chinese toys cost five times more than Indian ones
e: Market integration expands choices and lowers prices for consumers, while intense import competition can hurt local manufacturers.

q: What dilemma surrounds government policies like SEZ tax holidays and "flexibility in labour laws"?
o: While attracting foreign MNC investment and jobs, flexible hiring strips workers of job security, regular wages, and social benefits
They automatically double minimum wages for temporary staff
They drive all MNCs out of India
They instantly triple government tax collection
e: Tax holidays and flexible labour laws help woo MNCs, yet leave workers insecure; hence NCERT stresses proper enforcement of labour laws for fair globalisation.

q: How did improvements in BOTH transport and ICT together reshape service/magazine publishing for a London client in NCERT?
o: Text/instructions flow instantly from London to Delhi via internet -> designers in Delhi print and layout using telecom -> copies fly to London by cheap air transport -> payment settles instantly via e-banking
Manuscripts travel by ship taking six months
Payments are mailed in gold coins
Printing takes place strictly inside London
e: Combined IT/telecom, e-banking, and faster air transport allow services designed and printed in Delhi to serve London markets seamlessly at low cost.

q: US farmers receive massive government farm subsidies making their exports artificially cheap, while developing nations must remove barriers. Which stated ideal of the WTO does this violate?
o: The WTO ideal of free and fair international trade where rules apply equally rather than allowing developed countries to unfairly retain protections
The rule of raising 100% tariffs globally
Cash reserve ratio of banks
Domestic barter regulations
e: Though WTO is supposed to establish free and fair trade for all, in practice developed countries unfairly retained agricultural subsidies/barriers while pressuring developing nations.

q: How does the rise of Indian MNCs (Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy, Asian Paints, Sundaram Fasteners) show globalisation is NOT purely one-way?
o: Top Indian companies upgraded technology/standards and expanded operations globally—buying plants or serving clients worldwide as multinationals themselves
Indian companies banned foreign imports completely
Indian MNCs stopped operating outside India
Globalisation closed down Infosys
e: Just as foreign MNCs invest in India, competitive Indian firms leveraged globalisation to expand production and services across continents.

q: When giant MNC retail buyers force Indian garment exporters to bid rock-bottom prices, who bears the heaviest burden in the supply chain?
o: Workers at the bottom of the chain—through low temporary wages, long night shifts, and loss of social security—as exporters cut labour costs since raw material costs are fixed
Wealthy Western shoppers only
International shipping corporations
Central bank officials
e: Since costs of raw materials cannot be cut, Indian garment exporters squeeze labour costs by shifting from permanent staff to low-paid temporary workers.

q: How can government assist vulnerable small domestic producers (batteries, plastics, toys, tyres, capacitors) to withstand global competition without abruptly shutting down?
o: Providing cheap formal credit, better infrastructure, technical modernisation support, and temporary trade/investment barriers until they are strong enough to compete
Shutting down all domestic small units immediately
Doubling electricity tariffs on tiny factories
Encouraging dumping of cheap imports
e: Government can support small producers with cheap credit, reliable infrastructure, technology access, and strategic trade/investment barriers until they gain strength.

q:
Match the following events/terms with the globalisation concept they represent:
A. Cargill buying Parakh Foods
B. Use of shipping containers
C. 1991 removal of trade restrictions
D. Sushila shifting from permanent to temporary garment work
o: A-Foreign investment (MNC route), B-Transport technology improvement, C-Liberalisation, D-Uncertain employment impact on workers
A-Liberalisation, B-Foreign investment, C-Labour flexibility, D-Containerisation
A-Trade barrier, B-WTO farm subsidy, C-SEZ tax holiday, D-Import quota
A-Indian MNC, B-Cheque system, C-Banking, D-Agricultural loan
e: Cargill-Parakh (MNC investment), containers (transport technology), 1991 reforms (liberalisation), and Sushila (uncertain employment) match accurately.

q: What did Ford Motors’ export of 1,81,000 cars plus automobile components from India to South Africa, Mexico, Brazil, and USA demonstrate?
o: That MNCs integrated India not merely as a consumer market, but as a low-cost manufacturing and component-supplying hub for global operations
That zero cars were sold inside India
That Ford imported 100% of finished cars into Chennai
That Mahindra refused collaboration
e: Ford’s Chennai plant served domestic buyers while integrating India into global car and component supply chains across four continents.

q: What common objective is shared by India’s 1991 Liberalisation reforms and the creation of Special Economic Zones (SEZs)?
o: Encouraging foreign trade and attracting higher foreign investment (FDI) by reducing barriers, offering tax incentives, and improving infrastructure
Prohibiting MNCs from opening plants in India
Converting factories into farms
Raising import tariffs to 300%
e: Liberalisation removed trade/investment hurdles, while SEZs further incentivise foreign investment with world-class facilities, 5-year tax breaks, and labour flexibility.

q: Indian call centres working night shifts to handle daytime customer queries from the US or Europe illustrate which aspect of globalisation?
o: Cross-border real-time integration of IT-enabled services across time zones using low-cost skilled labour
Rising import quotas
Expansion of barter trade
WTO agricultural dispute
e: Affordable telecom, internet, and skilled English-speaking Indian youth make India an attractive global customer-care and IT outsourcing hub.

q: Globalisation widened consumer choices in India, yet why did urban well-off sections benefit far more than poor rural consumers?
o: Because well-off urban consumers have the purchasing power to buy diverse global brands, whereas poor households lack high income and many small producers/workers faced job insecurity or closures
Because rural residents are legally barred from shops
Because poor villagers buy luxury SUVs
Because cities lack retail markets
e: Benefits accrued disproportionately to well-off urban buyers and skilled elites, while low purchasing power and job/small-industry losses left many poor sections behind.

q: Which sector in India experienced dramatic global export growth during globalisation rather than shrinking under import competition?
o: Information Technology (IT), call centres, data entry, accounting, and engineering services
Small traditional toy workshops
Small capacitor factories
Small vegetable oil units
e: IT software companies like Infosys and service-exporting sectors (data entry, accounting, engineering) expanded rapidly globally.

q: Why do developing countries consistently demand at the WTO that developed countries eliminate their massive agricultural subsidies?

Ravi’s capacitors were twice as cheap as imports
e: Import liberalisation cut prices and widened options for buyers while simultaneously eroding tariff protection for vulnerable small producers like Ravi.

q: Which pair accurately contrasts a POSITIVE impact with a NEGATIVE impact of Globalisation in India?
o: Positive: Job growth in IT/component supply & rise of Indian MNCs like Tata Motors/Infosys; Negative: Crisis for small toy/capacitor producers & insecure temporary work like Sushila’s
Positive: Closure of small units; Negative: Wider consumer choice
Positive: Loss of worker PF; Negative: Growth of Infosys
Positive: Elimination of broadband; Negative: Lower port costs
e: This pair accurately summarises both sides documented in NCERT: gains for consumers, top Indian firms, and IT/component jobs versus hardship for small manufacturers and temporary workers.

q: When an MNC like Ford invests Rs 1,700 crore to build a large plant in India and exports 1,81,000 cars plus components worldwide, what economic impact does this generate?
o: Foreign exchange earnings via exports, fresh demand for local component suppliers, modern manufacturing technology transfer, and new employment
Zero local suppliers can sell components
Domestic car buyers lose all choices
Infrastructure spending stops across Tamil Nadu
e: Export-oriented FDI brings capital, modern production methods, export earnings, and orders for local component suppliers.

q: Would reversing globalisation completely back to 1950s isolationism be the best response to job insecurity and small-producer struggles? What does NCERT advocate instead?
o: No; rather than rejecting global integration altogether, NCERT calls for a struggle for "Fair Globalisation"—enforcing labour laws, supporting small producers, and negotiating fairer WTO rules
Yes, close all ports, airports, and internet services immediately
Yes, ban Tata Motors and Infosys from operating abroad
No, because temporary workers should have zero legal protections
e: Globalisation is a reality; the goal proposed in NCERT is not isolationism but making globalisation fairer so opportunities and gains are shared widely.

q:
Arrange these milestones from NCERT in chronological order:
1. India imposing trade barriers to shield nascent industries
2. India introducing economic liberalisation
3. Ford Motors arriving in India and setting up its Chennai plant
4. Removal of import restrictions on capacitors hitting Ravi’s unit
e: Post-Independence protection (1950s–60s) -> Liberalisation (1991) -> Ford Motors Chennai plant (1995) -> Capacitor import restriction removal (2001).

q: Small Indian producers fail to match imported quality or costs largely because they lack capital and modern technology. Combining "Money and Credit" (ch_13) and "Globalisation" (ch_14), what solution emerges?
o: Providing cheap, accessible formal credit from banks and cooperatives enables small domestic producers to upgrade technology and machinery so they can compete fairly in a globalised market
Small workshops should rely on 60% moneylenders
All domestic banks should halt small business loans
Only MNCs deserve RBI credit oversight
e: Affordable formal credit empowers small domestic producers to modernise technology, raise quality, and withstand global competition.

q: Which steps mentioned in NCERT for achieving Fair Globalisation keep small producers afloat without abandoning trade altogether?
o: Supporting small producers to improve performance until strong enough, using trade and investment barriers if necessary, and negotiating fairer WTO rules with fellow developing nations
Halting all international trade permanently
Doubling taxes on small domestic workshops
Halving factory worker wages
e: Domestic support until small firms strengthen, strategic use of barriers where needed, and collective WTO negotiation form the core agenda of Fair Globalisation.

q: Are MNCs ALWAYS harmful to every local Indian producer? Identify the INCORRECT statement:
o: Takeovers like Cargill buying Parakh Foods created stiff competition for domestic rivals
Cheap imports severely hurt small independent units like Ravi’s capacitor plant
Many local companies supplying components and raw materials to MNCs actually prospered and expanded
Globalisation created zero new jobs in India and prevented any Indian firm from operating abroad
e: Globalisation did generate new jobs in IT, electronics, automobiles, and supplier firms, and propelled several Indian firms into becoming MNCs.

q: Why are containerisation and the internet considered the twin pillars of modern Global Supply Chains?
o: Containers move physical components and finished goods across oceans cheaply and safely, while the internet coordinates designs, orders, banking, and services instantaneously
Containers carry IT data while internet moves heavy steel
Ships disappeared after the internet arrived
Both serve only rural agriculture
e: Low-cost physical freight via containers/airlines plus instantaneous digital coordination via IT/internet power global production networks.

q: Which NCERT example clearly illustrates that foreign MNC entry can lead to foreign control over established Indian domestic brands and assets?
o: US MNC Cargill Foods acquiring Indian Parakh Foods along with its established brand, marketing network, and four refineries to dominate edible oil output
Sundaram Fasteners manufacturing bolts in Chennai
Indian Post running rural post offices
Ravi employing 7 workers in Hosur
e: Cargill’s takeover of Parakh Foods shows how cash-rich MNCs acquire existing local brands, networks, and refineries.

q: NCERT notes India’s 1991 liberalisation policy was supported by powerful international organisations advocating free trade and global integration. Which body formally oversees trade rules worldwide today?
o: World Trade Organisation (WTO)
International Olympic Committee
Greenpeace International
SAARC Postal Union
e: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) is the global institution initiated by developed countries to push removal of trade barriers and set international trade rules.

q: Why is the developed countries’ opposition at the WTO to developing-country farm protections criticised as hypocrisy in NCERT?
o: Because developed countries violate free-trade principles themselves by heavily subsidising their own tiny (~0.5%) farm sector while demanding developing countries eliminate all barriers
Because developing countries have no farmers
Because the US has completely zero farm subsidies
Because WTO bans developing nations from exporting
e: NCERT asks "Is this free and fair trade?"—highlighting the double standard where rich nations preserve massive subsidies while forcing poor nations to drop barriers.

q: Accurately separate the Indian groups into "Largely Benefited" vs "Severely Challenged" by globalisation based on NCERT:
o: Benefited: Well-off urban consumers, large Indian firms (Tata Motors, Infosys), skilled elites; Challenged: Small domestic producers (batteries, capacitors, toys) and flexible temporary export workers
Benefited: Small toy makers and temporary workers; Challenged: Infosys and Tata Motors
Both gained identically
Neither group experienced any change
e: Urban well-off consumers, top Indian firms, and skilled elites gained substantially, while small manufacturers and flexible/temporary workers faced severe pressure.

q: Why does Globalisation extend beyond mere movement of physical goods?
o: Because globalisation integrates economies through cross-border flows of services (IT, call centres), foreign investments, technology, and migration of people seeking jobs/education
Because only grain crosses oceans
Because MNCs remain confined to one city
Because internet ends international links
e: Alongside goods, cross-border flows of services, investments, technology, and movement of people collectively drive globalisation.

q: In the same Indian city, an educated youth earns well at an MNC call centre while Sushila loses permanent benefits and works night shifts as a temporary garment worker. What does this contrast prove?
o: Globalisation generated sharply uneven outcomes within India—rewarding skilled, educated workers in IT/services while pushing less-skilled workers into flexible, insecure jobs
India has no garment exports
Call centres are unregulated informal workshops
Sushila gained lifetime pension benefits
e: NCERT emphasises that people with education, skill, and wealth seized new opportunities, while many workers faced heightened insecurity.

q: If an MNC threatens to relocate to another country as soon as its 5-year SEZ tax holiday expires or wages rise slightly, what characteristic of MNCs does this expose?
o: MNCs are highly mobile in search of lowest production costs and tax breaks—underscoring the need for durable domestic skills/infrastructure and collective labour-standard enforcement
MNCs operate purely as charitable trusts
MNCs can never move factories internationally
MNCs ignore production costs completely
e: Because MNCs relentlessly seek lowest costs and tax breaks across borders, nations need strong domestic infrastructure, skills, and firm labour-law enforcement.

q:
Consider these three statements about the WTO:
1. It was started at the initiative of developed countries.
2. Its aim is to liberalise international trade and establish trade rules.
3. In practice, it has completely eliminated US/European farm subsidies and always favoured poor farmers.
Which statements are true?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
All 1, 2 and 3
e: Statements 1 and 2 are true; statement 3 is false because developed nations continue paying massive farm subsidies while pressuring developing nations.

q: To help Indian toy makers recover market share lost to Chinese toys (which took 70–80% of shops), which two measures would work best together?
o: Combining cheap formal credit and modern design/tech upgrades to improve cost-quality competitiveness WITH selective temporary tariff/quality barriers until domestic units strengthen
Shutting down all toy shops + raising bank interest to 60%
Returning to barter exchange
Banning all plastics inside factories
e: Pairing cheap formal credit and design/tech modernisation with selective protection gives small domestic manufacturers breathing room to regain competitiveness.

q: Counterfactual analysis: Had India retained rigid 1960s trade/investment barriers after 1991 without liberalisation, what would have been the likely outcome for Indian consumers and firms like Infosys?
o: Consumers would remain limited to few domestic models with lower quality/choice, inward FDI would stay minimal, and firms like Infosys/Tata Motors would struggle to scale globally
Indian IT exports would have grown ten times faster without global links
Every household would own imported cars
Domestic producers would automatically achieve world-leading standards without competition
e: The 1991 shift recognised that prolonged isolation would deprive consumers of quality/choice and prevent competitive Indian firms from reaching global markets.

q: Why does the concluding section of NCERT’s "Globalisation and the Indian Economy" highlight campaigns by people’s organisations?
o: To demonstrate that achieving Fair Globalisation is a struggle in which citizens, workers, and people’s organisations play a vital role—having even influenced major WTO trade/investment decisions
To argue that citizens have zero influence over international trade
To prove MNCs voluntarily enforce labour rights
To show WTO only deals with sports
e: NCERT concludes that citizens and people’s organisations play an important role in the struggle for fair globalisation, having already influenced key WTO decisions.

q: What common thread links 1991 Liberalisation, containerisation, SEZs, and WTO membership in Class 10 Economics?
o: All four are key drivers, policies, or institutions shaping India’s integration into the world economy (Globalisation) through expanded foreign trade and FDI
All four aimed to restore the barter system
All four deal with local Panchayati Raj elections
All four are methods of printing currency notes
e: Transport technology (containers), domestic policy reforms (1991 liberalisation & SEZs), and global governance (WTO) together shape Globalisation.

q: What is the overarching conclusion of the chapter "Globalisation and the Indian Economy"?
o: Globalisation accelerated integration through MNCs, technology, and liberalisation, yet its benefits remain uneven—requiring strong labour-law enforcement, support for small producers, and fairer WTO rules to achieve Fair Globalisation
Only casual temporary workers benefited while urban consumers suffered
Every country must permanently ban all foreign trade
MNCs operate without profit motives
e: Rather than opposing global links blindly, the core takeaway is making globalisation fairer through labour protection, support to small producers, and equitable WTO governance.
